target.statement: QPA descends toward latest overflow deadline d^Δ for unschedulable sets and toward zero for schedulable sets if the early stopping condition is relaxed.

issues.description: Several upper-bound expressions divide by 1-U, while their surrounding iff statements include U<=1; when U=1 those formulas do not evaluate.
The predecessor pseudocode computes an earlier deadline than t when equal to t, but surrounding prose describes a maximum deadline at or before t.
Lemma 5 proof uses t^Δ in one inequality although the overflow threshold defined elsewhere is d^Δ.
QPA initializes t with max{d_i|d_i<L} and scans for a previous deadline, but the supplied evidence does not explicitly handle an empty candidate set.
Busy-period iteration gives a fixed-point stopping condition but no explicit behavior for an iteration that does not reach a finite fixed point.

nodes.value: Hard real-time, independent periodic and/or sporadic tasks scheduled by preemptive EDF on a uniprocessor; relative deadlines may differ from periods.
nodes.notes: The one-processor setting is stated in the abstract and EDF discussion; the system model itself also describes EDF preemption.

nodes.value: The set {τ_1,τ_2,...,τ_n} of n independent real-time tasks.
A task τ_i, periodic or sporadic, comprising an infinite or finite stream of jobs.
A released request or job of a task that must complete by its deadline.
One processor serving jobs under EDF.
A schedule dispatching a pending job with the earliest absolute deadline.
Interval during which the processor is busy.
Number of tasks n.
Worst-case execution requirement C_i per job of task τ_i; C_i>0.
Relative deadline D_i shared by jobs of task τ_i; may be less than, equal to, or greater than T_i.
T_i is the exact periodic interarrival time or the sporadic minimum interarrival time.
nodes.notes: Same notation, different arrival guarantee for periodic and sporadic tasks.

nodes.value: A job released at t has absolute deadline t+D_i.
nodes.notes: The symbol d_i also represents enumerated deadlines kT_i+D_i later; those are presented as analysis candidates.

nodes.value: Time instant or interval length t as specified by the surrounding demand expression or algorithm.
nodes.notes: Not all occurrences of t have the same role; keep argument scopes distinct.

nodes.value: Index k used to enumerate candidate absolute deadlines.
nodes.notes: Whether ℕ includes zero is not made explicit in the evidence.

nodes.value: Utilization of task τ_i.
Sum of the task utilizations.
The real-time tasks are independent.
Every task job must complete execution before its deadline.
Every job of task τ_i requires no more than its task worst-case execution time C_i.
All jobs of the same task share the task relative deadline D_i.
Preemption is allowed at any time; an earlier-deadline job may preempt a later-deadline job.
An arrived, pending job with earliest absolute deadline is selected for execution.
The main analysis does not constrain D_i relative to T_i.
Candidate analysis deadlines are of the form d_i=kT_i+D_i with k∈ℕ.
nodes.notes: This is the candidate deadline formula used by demand analysis; sporadic jobs need not actually release at every such point.

nodes.value: Maximum execution-time requirement of jobs whose releases and deadlines both lie within one contiguous interval of length t.
nodes.label: Equation (1)

nodes.label: Equation (4)
nodes.notes: This redefines L_a compared with (2); context and equation label distinguish the two. Undefined at U=1.

nodes.label: Definition 1

Initialize busy-period iteration by summing all task costs.

nodes.label: Equation (6)

Compute L_b by initializing w^0, iterating the ceiling recurrence, and stopping at its fixed point.
nodes.notes: The source specifies the fixed-point stopping condition but no separate handling of a nonconvergent sequence.

nodes.value: Piecewise QPA upper horizon uses min(L_a,L_b) when U<1 and L_b when U=1.
nodes.label: Equation (7)
nodes.notes: L_a is not defined at U=1. This equation does not specify behavior for U>1 (which fails utilization check).

nodes.value: Smallest task relative deadline.
For an unschedulable system, the latest candidate deadline strictly within (0,L) at which h(d_i)>d_i.
nodes.notes: Definition presupposes an overflow deadline in the specified interval; the source connects this to exact schedulability.

nodes.value: Largest candidate absolute deadline strictly smaller than L.
Smallest absolute deadline larger than d^Δ in Lemma 4.
Processor demand h(t) is nondecreasing in its interval-length argument.
nodes.notes: Stated in the proof, not separately proved in the Evidence Layer.

nodes.value: For an unschedulable system with d_m=max{d_i|d_i<L} and h(d_m)<=d_m, d^Δ<h(d^Δ)<d′, where d′ is the next deadline after d^Δ.
nodes.label: Lemma 4

nodes.value: For an unschedulable system with h(d_m)<=d_m, all t∈[h(d^Δ),d_m) satisfy h(d^Δ)<=h(t)<=t.
nodes.label: Lemma 5

nodes.value: Descending iterative schedulability algorithm: initialize t at the largest deadline below L; while h(t)<=t and h(t)>d_min, replace t by h(t) if strictly smaller or by the preceding deadline if equal; decide by h(t)<=d_min.
nodes.notes: Algorithm of Theorem 5. This is mathematical pseudocode, not a verified implementation. Precheck U<=1 is in the theorem, outside the displayed pseudocode.

nodes.value: Initialize the descending search at the largest candidate deadline strictly below L.
Continue while processor demand does not exceed current t and remains above the minimum relative deadline.
If h(t)<t, update t to h(t).
Otherwise in the loop, when h(t)=t, update t to the greatest candidate deadline strictly below t.
The algorithm returns schedulable if h(t)<=d_min; otherwise not schedulable.
If an unschedulable task set has h(d_m)>d_m, the algorithm immediately stops on the overflow condition.
When h(d_m)<=d_m, the proof uses d_m>d^Δ and divides the descent into three cases.
Case 1 (h(t)<t): using monotonicity and Lemma 5, the t←h(t) step keeps t at least h(d^Δ).
Case 2 (h(t)=t): the preceding deadline step stays at or above d^Δ; choosing d^Δ exposes an overflow, otherwise the process repeats.
Case 3 (t=h(d^Δ)): the next earlier deadline is d^Δ and the algorithm stops because h(d^Δ)>d^Δ.
For every unschedulable task set the iteration maintains h(t)>=h(d^Δ)>d^Δ>=d_min, so stopping with h(t)<=d_min implies schedulability.
nodes.notes: This is the stated direction of the source proof; the theorem asserts an iff result.

nodes.value: QPA descends toward latest overflow deadline d^Δ for unschedulable sets and toward zero for schedulable sets if the early stopping condition is relaxed.
nodes.notes: Qualitative algorithm behavior stated in the paper; not a complexity guarantee.

nodes.value: For τ_j with D_j<t, the source gives the release time of its last job with deadline no later than t.
For task τ_j with D_j<t, last absolute deadline at or before t is floor((t-D_j)/T_j)T_j+D_j.
nodes.label: Equation (8)

nodes.value: If latest per-task deadline equals t, subtract T_j to obtain a strictly earlier deadline.
d_max^t starts at zero and is updated to the largest eligible adjusted d_j in the per-task scan.
Scan j=1,...,n; if D_j<t compute candidate deadline (8), step backward by T_j when equal to t, and retain the largest adjusted d_j.
nodes.notes: Pseudocode implements a STRICT predecessor via d_j=t adjustment; E076/E079 call the result a non-strict maximum (<=t), which is inconsistent in boundary cases.

nodes.notes: Do not silently change <= to < in source claims. The QPA algorithm needs the strict predecessor branch. At t equal to a deadline, the two operations differ.
